Courland
koor'land
n. (the Baltic duchy west of the Daugava, Lutheran from its founding in 1561 and the one piece of Livonia that survived the wars)
From the tribal name of the Curonians, latinised Curonia, with German Land; the land of the Curs.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Courland is the western part of modern Latvia, between the Daugava and the sea. When the Livonian confederation collapsed under Russian attack, the last Master of the Livonian Order, Gotthard Kettler, submitted to Poland in 1561, dissolved the Order, and took Courland and Semgallia as a hereditary Lutheran duchy for himself and his heirs. He got what Albert of Prussia had got thirty-six years earlier and by much the same means. The duchy lasted until 1795 and was consistently Lutheran: Kettler's ordinances of 1567 required a church and a school in every parish, the visitations enforced them, and a Curonian peasantry that had been nominally Christian for three centuries began to be catechised. Courland is the small, durable survival out of a general wreck. Proverbs gives the test by which such a state is measured: “When the righteous are in authority, the people rejoice: but when the wicked beareth rule, the people mourn” (Pro 29:2).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a duchy as the territory of a duke; a visitation as the official visit of a superior to inspect the state of a church or district; and authority as legal power, the right to command.

expand to see more

DUCHY, n. The territory or dominions of a duke; a dukedom.

VISITATION, n. The act of visiting; the official visit of a superior to a church or district for the purpose of inspection and correction.

AUTHORITY, n. [L. auctoritas.] Legal power, or a right to command or to act; the power of a ruler.

PARISH, n. The precinct or territorial jurisdiction of a secular priest, or the township committed to his charge.

REJOICE, v.i. To experience joy and gladness in a high degree; to be exhilarated with lively and pleasurable sensations.

Key Scripture

Pro 29:2 — "When the righteous are in authority, the people rejoice: but when the wicked beareth rule, the people mourn."

Rom 13:3 — "For rulers are not a terror to good works, but to the evil. Wilt thou then not be afraid of the power? do that which is good, and thou shalt have praise of the same:"

Psa 72:11 — "Yea, all kings shall fall down before him: all nations shall serve him."

2Ch 31:21 — "And in every work that he began in the service of the house of God, and in the law, and in the commandments, to seek his God, he did it with all his heart, and prospered."

Modern Corruption

The Baltic duchy founded in 1561 when Gotthard Kettler dissolved the Livonian Order; Lutheran throughout, with a church and school required in every parish from 1567.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The honest reckoning with Courland is about serfdom. Kettler's ordinances gave every parish a church and a school, and the same century bound the Curonian and Latvian peasantry more tightly to the land than they had been under the Order. A duchy can require catechism in every village and still hold its catechumens as property, and Courland did. The dictionary records the schools as a real good and refuses to let them stand as the whole account.

The principle to recover is that rule is to be measured by what happens to the ruled. Proverbs supplies the test and it is not stability or revenue: “When the righteous are in authority, the people rejoice: but when the wicked beareth rule, the people mourn” (Pro 29:2). Paul states the ruler's proper direction — “For rulers are not a terror to good works, but to the evil” (Rom 13:3) — and the ultimate subjection of every ruler is already written: “Yea, all kings shall fall down before him: all nations shall serve him” (Psa 72:11). Hezekiah is the standard of a prince's reform: he did it “with all his heart, and prospered” (2Ch 31:21).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew mashal (H4910), to rule or have dominion; Greek archon (G758), a ruler.

Hebrew mashal (H4910) — to rule, to have dominion; “when the wicked beareth rule”, Proverbs 29:2.

Hebrew samach (H8055) — to rejoice, to be glad; Proverbs 29:2.

Hebrew 'anach (H584) — to sigh, to groan, to mourn; Proverbs 29:2.

Greek archon (G758) — a ruler, a chief, a magistrate; Romans 13:3.

Hebrew tsalach (H6743) — to prosper, to succeed; 2 Chronicles 31:21.

Usage

"“When the righteous are in authority, the people rejoice” (Pro 29:2) — a church and a school required in every parish from 1567."

"“For rulers are not a terror to good works, but to the evil” (Rom 13:3) — a Lutheran duchy that nevertheless bound its peasantry as serfs."

"“to seek his God, he did it with all his heart, and prospered” (2Ch 31:21) — the duchy stood from 1561 to 1795."
